To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the efficacy of the anti-R mutant antiserum is not significantly different from that of normal sera; (2) the variable efficacy of the anti- R mutant antiserum cannot be explained by differences in virulence of the inocula.

“In mice infected with a serum-resistant Escherichia colistrain, the protective efficacy of normal rabbit sera and hyperimmune sera to the J5 rough mutant of E. coli was not statistically significantly different, provided the same rabbit was the source of the preimmune and the hyperimmune sera.”
In summary, our research is concerned with
the immunoprophylaxis of gram-negative bacterial infections in animals.
the role of the immune response in the pathogenesis of gram-negative bacteremia, particularly in the development of septic shock.
the immunological basis of the host resistance to bacterial infection and with the development of a vaccine for the prevention of gram-negative bacteremia in man.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the immunization of mice with rough mutant antisera does not protect the mice against lethal gram-negative sepsis and that the immunization does not enhance the protective effect of normal sera.
there is a limited protective effect of the anti-JS antisera against the bacteremia induced by the 06:KZ:H1 strain ofE. coli in the mouse model.
the immunoprotective effect of anti-J5 sera is not significantly different from that of normal sera in the prevention of experimental gram-negative bacterial infections in mice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the protective efficacy in mice of the J5 antiserum does not differ significantly from that of preimmune sera, provided that the donor rabbits are the same.
the J5 vaccine has been shown to be effective in preventing gram-negative infections in mice, dogs, and humans, but not in all species.
the protective effects of anti-rough mutant sera against gram-negative bacteremia are limited.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of rough mutants as vaccines is unlikely to be a successful strategy.
it is not enough to simply have a vaccine.
the anti-rough antibody response to the vaccine strain is not sufficient to prevent the development of bacteremia in the face of a lethal challenge with a serum-resistant strain ofE. coli.
